title: Pose Estimation
description: Heatmap-based keypoint detection for reconstructing body pose from an image.
subject: dl
html:
Pose estimation detects the specific location of an articulated body's keypoints — joints like elbows, knees, shoulders, and wrists — reconstructing a person's (or animal's) skeletal pose from a single image.

The Task, Precisely

For each keypoint of interest (e.g. left elbow, right knee), predict its \((x,y)\) location in the image — typically for a fixed, predefined set of keypoints (e.g. 17 for a common human pose standard: nose, eyes, ears, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles).

The Heatmap-Based Approach

Rather than directly regressing raw \((x,y)\) coordinates, most modern pose estimation models predict a heatmap per keypoint — a spatial probability map the same size as (or a downsampled version of) the input image, where the highest-intensity pixel indicates the model's predicted keypoint location. This heatmap framing (very similar in spirit to segmentation's per-pixel output) tends to train more stably and accurately than directly regressing coordinate values.

Diagram

Detected keypoints (joints) are connected into a skeletal structure representing the estimated body pose.

Code

import torchvision.models.detection as detection_models

model = detection_models.keypointrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights='DEFAULT')
model.eval()

x = [torch.randn(3, 480, 640)]
predictions = model(x)
print(predictions[0]['keypoints'].shape)   # (num_people_detected, num_keypoints, 3) -- x, y, visibility per keypoint

Common Mistakes

  • Directly regressing raw \((x,y)\) coordinates instead of using a heatmap representation — heatmap-based prediction is generally more robust and easier to train, since it frames the problem more like a familiar per-pixel (segmentation-style) task rather than a harder direct-regression problem.
  • Forgetting to handle occluded or out-of-frame keypoints — real pose estimation systems must predict a visibility/confidence score per keypoint, not just assume every keypoint is always visible.

Interview Relevance

Q: "Why do modern pose estimation models predict heatmaps rather than directly regressing keypoint coordinates?" Heatmap prediction frames the problem as a per-pixel probability task, similar to segmentation, which tends to train more stably and produce more accurate localization than directly regressing raw coordinate values — a heatmap can express a smooth, spatially-structured confidence distribution around the true keypoint location, which is harder to represent with a single regressed coordinate pair alone.

Practice Question

Why must a practical pose estimation system predict a confidence or visibility score per keypoint, in addition to its location?
